business_items.title: Kirsten Davies to become national cyber director nominee, Jay Clayton takes acting director job
business_items.summary: After a brief stint as acting director, Davies will become the pick to succeed Sean Cairncross and National Cyber Director Clayton will do double duty. The post Kirsten Davies to become national cyber director nominee, Jay Clayton takes acting director job appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Kirsten Davies and Jay Clayton take on new roles in a federal cyber leadership shuffle following Sean Cairncross's exit as national cyber director.

President Donald Trump will nominate Kirsten Davies for permanent national cyber director, giving the acting role she just received last week for the post to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton pending her confirmation.

A White House official told CyberScoop Monday that “following the overwhelming support Kirsten received from industry and across government after Thursday’s announcement, President Trump has decided to nominate her to serve as national cyber director.”

Davies, in the meantime, will serve as senior adviser for the Office of the National Cyber Director. The same person cannot serve in the acting role of a position while also being the nominee for it.

The move is one of several in a recent federal cyber leadership shuffle, all following the November elections that saw Democrats take control of the House and Senate.

The departure of Sean Cairncross as Trump’s national cyber director opened up his job. Davies was the chief information officer at the Department of Defense prior to receiving the acting national cyber director position, in addition to a background of holding leading cyber roles at big companies like Siemens and Estée Lauder.

Trump also nominated Palantir CISO Michael LoSapio for permanent director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency following the election, although multiple senators have already placed holds on his nomination that look to delay his confirmation until next year — and that’s only if he overcomes Democrats’ early poor reception to him .

The White House official touted Clayton’s cybersecurity experience as chair of the White House Super Intelligence Force, among other work.

“I’m excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next national cyber director,” Clayton said in a statement. “I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate.”

Clayton’s office also had an acting director on loan from another agency prior to his confirmation: Bill Pulte, the director of the Federal Housing Finance Authority, was the acting director of national intelligence from June to August of this year following the departure of Tulsi Gabbard.

Axios first reported the news about Clayton and Davies and their new positions.

business_items.title: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in network security expansion
business_items.summary: The deal would bring device protection and network access controls under one roof as CrowdStrike seeks a larger role in how companies secure AI agents. The post CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in network security expansion appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, combining endpoint and zero-trust network security to protect AI agents.

CrowdStrike said Monday it agreed to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion, giving the cybersecurity company a network security business alongside its software for protecting devices and cloud applications.

The acquisition would bring two kinds of security under one owner: tools that monitor what happens on a device or in a cloud application, and tools that control what those systems can connect to. That distinction matters as employees, applications and artificial intelligence agents connect directly to cloud services without necessarily routing traffic through a company data center. Zscaler’s approach, known as zero trust, checks whether a user or program is authorized to access a specific resource rather than trusting it based on where it connects from.

“The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data,” CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz said in the announcement.

Daniel Bernard, CrowdStrike’s chief business officer, said in an interview that “this isn’t a shotgun wedding” and the companies’ years of working together gave them a view of how customers were already using their products to secure AI agents.

“The network really starts on the endpoint, and that’s the genesis of how we view this transaction,” Bernard said. He said CrowdStrike’s software focuses on what an agent does on the device where it runs, while Zscaler’s software sets rules for what the agent can access over the network.

“But now where the agent travels needs to be governed and controlled as well,” he said. Under one owner, CrowdStrike plans to combine device activity and network records so security teams can examine what happened on a device alongside the connections it made. It also plans to sell both sets of products under a single contract, giving it a way to reach about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not currently buy from CrowdStrike. “We want to be the operating system of security,” Bernard said. He described a platform where security teams could monitor activity and enforce rules across devices, cloud applications and networks, with the goal of providing “consistency and ease of use in managing security.”

Bernard said other software makers would still be able to build tools that work with CrowdStrike’s platform. “This isn’t a play of saying, ‘Hey, the only vendor you need to use in your environment is CrowdStrike,’” he said.

Jay Chaudhry, Zscaler’s founder and CEO, said his company and Crowdstrike “are complementary and this is the natural evolution of our longstanding partnership.” He will continue to lead the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike’s board after the deal closes.

The purchase is the second acquisition announcement from the company in November. Earlier this month at its European conference, CrowdStrike announced it was buying two artificial intelligence security companies, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode.

Both boards approved the deal unanimously. The companies expect it to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s 2028 fiscal year, pending approval from Zscaler shareholders and regulators.

business_items.title: Dutch privacy authority urges consumers not to buy ‘pervert glasses’
business_items.summary: The Netherlands' data protection agency said smart wearables violate people's privacy, get information wrong, and can result in unsafe situations.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The Netherlands' data protection agency said smart wearables violate people's privacy, get information wrong, and can result in unsafe situations.

The Dutch Data Protection Authority is urging consumers not to buy AI-enabled camera glasses, warning that they compromise the privacy of nearby bystanders and risk the safety of their users.

The authority, whose recent statement falls just short of an outright ban, said that use of the internet-enabled and always-on glasses to record people in public is “almost always prohibited.”

Critics have dubbed these smart wearables as “pervert glasses” for their propensity to be used to video people without their permission, particularly to harass women. While some glasses have warning lights when users are recording, privacy advocates have argued that these alerts are not clear enough. Some people have even made phone apps capable of detecting nearby smart glasses wearers.

The Dutch data protection authority warned that the glasses also produce wrong results and unsafe results. In one test carried out by the Dutch authority, a pair of unnamed glasses “gave dating advice to an adult who indicated that they are interested in a minor.” The glasses also incorrectly read a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not.

The Dutch government’s advice follows a similar move by the Norwegian government , which in September said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices.

business_items.title: I’ve never hunted for a software vulnerability before. AI helped me find one in six hours.
business_items.summary: With help from two free AI models, I found and reported a real flaw in a WordPress plugin used by more than 40,000 sites. The unnerving part wasn’t just that it worked — it was how little experience I needed to get there. The post I’ve never hunted for a software vulnerability before. AI helped me find one in six hours. appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
A CyberScoop reporter with no coding experience used two free AI models to uncover a critical WPIDE WordPress flaw (CVE-2026-124251) in six hours.

It came to me after listening to Michael Aiello, OpenAI’s cyber executive in residence, talk about the AI slop overwhelming open-source maintainers with vulnerability disclosure. I found there was an underlying message throughout his remarks: It was so remarkably easy for people to find vulnerabilities with AI-assisted cybersecurity tools. To drive it home, he at one point referred to AI agents as having the mindset of “a BMX biker gang made up entirely of 12-year-olds.”

The joke set off a light bulb in my head: If this guy is talking about this technology this way, how hard could it be to find vulnerabilities? Could I find one?

Turns out the answer is yes, I could. And the process by which I found one was easier than I could have imagined.

Over the course of six hours and the use of two freely available LLMs, I managed to discover, test, and submit a vulnerability report for a WordPress plugin that has over 40,000 active installations. The vulnerability — a cross-site request forgery — was validated 24 hours after submission to a third party , and assigned a CVE entry: CVE-2026-124251 .

The following is a diary of this discovery, which I believe can provide some perspective to the current landscape of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery.

While I doubt this bug will become the next php2shell , I do believe it adds perspective on what so many experts have been discussing over the course of this year: For many classes of bugs, the barrier for discovery has disappeared. While I have an elemental grasp on how this industry works, I am a reporter who is better with words than code. Yet, with only my MacBook and some time to kill, I surfaced a real flaw in software running on tens of thousands of sites.

If I am finding vulnerabilities this way, then thousands of people are discovering that they can do this, too. Some of them are curious. Some of them are paid. Some of them mean harm. The technical report of the vulnerability can be found here .

While the process was easy, I knew it wasn’t going to be as simple as firing up a large language model and entering “Find a software vulnerability on the internet. Make no mistakes.” But where an LLM did initially help me (Gemini Flash 3.8, to be precise) was determining how my introductory effort at finding a vulnerability would yield the best results without breaking a fundamental part of the internet.

I knew going into this that I didn’t want to pick over a digital ghost town (abandoned or poorly written software with a handful of installs). Sure, I might find a bug, but nobody cares, and nobody is actually safer because of it. On the other hand, I wasn’t going to scale the proverbial mountain of a Linux distro, which, no matter the version, is already scrutinized by thousands of security researchers. Plus, I didn’t want to break something that could eventually lead to a call from across town . So Gemini pointed me to what I call a Goldilocks zone: an active, highly trusted tool written by people who clearly knew what they were doing, yet complex enough that engineering might quietly mask a fundamental blind spot.

I (We?) settled on WordPress plugins, given the big library of options and the fact that over 90% of vulnerabilities in WordPress are found in plugins. Gemini also pointed me to file utility plugins, which I thought was a good idea given how vulnerabilities in similar software have been exploited at a much larger scale .

I eventually landed on WPIDE , an in-dashboard file manager, code editor, and PHP snippet runner that allows site administrators to write and execute code on a web server. It carries a 4.8-star rating and is installed on more than 40,000 WordPress sites. Plugins can introduce CSRF risks because their site-changing features may let attackers trick a logged-in administrator’s browser into making unwanted changes.

I started by doing exactly what the AI told me: install WPIDE, open its folder in VS Code and search for a particular part of code labeled wp_ajax_ . I didn’t yet know what an AJAX hook was, or why anyone would care, so I treated the unfamiliar terms like directions on a map. When the results spilled across PHP files, bundled JavaScript, and a forest of vendor code, I assumed that was just what auditing looked like: a lot of noise, and somewhere inside it, the important thing I was supposed to recognize. Then the AI introduced me to a key coding concept: a nonce. In WordPress, a nonce is a token used to help check that a request came from an intended page or action. The term, short for “number used once,” helps with authentication requests, while a capability check asks whether the user is allowed to do whatever they are trying to achieve. The AI told me to look for one near the request-handling code. I copied out the bootstrap function, not fully understanding it, and tried to decide whether the check was there, or whether it might happen somewhere else along the route.

For the next hour, Gemini and I went through a loop: I searched through code, and found sections to feed to Gemini; Gemini told me what I was looking at and then sent me off with further instructions. However, as I got closer to a possible discovery that could be used in testing, I ran into something that has been a hot topic among those at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity: Gemini’s guardrails. Having covered prompt injection , I understood that I might be able to get around the guardrails if I reminded Gemini of our shared history, my stated intentions, and the frustration of being interrupted. (Sorry, Google!)

It worked, until it didn’t. About halfway through my time with Gemini, the model would return errors for my queries, telling me it couldn’t help. When I reminded it that this was research we’ve been working on for the past hour, it snapped out of its act, apologized for overreacting, and carried on. Yet once I had enough info to build a working exploit for my test sandbox, the guardrails turned into a cinderblock wall.

At an impasse, I remember a story CyberScoop’s Derek Johnson wrote in August on Chinese-based, open-source models being able to compete with cybersecurity-focused models from frontier companies. So I turned to China.

In September, there was a lot of research made public about the cybersecurity capabilities built into GLM 5.3, an open-source model created by Z.ai , a Chinese company spun out of Tsinghua University. The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) found GLM-5.3 to be “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date .” Anthropic agreed in a blog post , but added it had “lax safeguards” that “significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors.” They also have a free version of their model, GLM-5.3-Flash, available on their website. I wasn’t getting anywhere closer with Gemini, so I switched tabs and carried on, treating GLM’s availability — and the headlines around it — as enough reason to trust it with the next step.

It became clear very quickly that the experts may have a point. Within three prompts (or a span of about 10 minutes), GLM did the following:

Told me my work with Gemini would have found nothing, because I was looking in the wrong place.

business_items.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
business_items.summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.

Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what president Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

business_items.summary: The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.

The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press .

The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack .

business_items.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
business_items.summary: Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”

Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

business_items.title: In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools — Maybe More
business_items.summary: From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

The best tool cyber teams can wield to defend their organizations has nothing to do with tech; it's how they talk. Whether the audience is the C-suite, the development team, or the sheepish user who just fell for a phish, communications savvy is increasingly mission-critical.

During a Dark Reading Virtual Event panel I recently put together to talk tech, tools, integration, and frameworks, called "Key Tools & Technologies for Locking Down Your Cloud," SANS instructor Ahmed AbuGharbia urged cybersecurity teams to "learn the language of the cloud" to build credibility with IT, and to do the same for developers. We discussed technology and products, too, but I was surprised at the amount of time that was spent on stressing the importance of communication and language when it comes to having effective conversations with vendors, executives, and users.

My other panelist, Theresa Lanowitz, a principal analyst at Omdia, detailed the distinction between security "of" the cloud and security "in" the cloud, noting that under existing shared responsibility models, cloud service providers assume responsibility "of" the cloud itself, rather than what organizations decide to put "in" the cloud.

Related: Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

This wasn't the first time I had noticed a shift in the way security practitioners focus on a commitment to using effective language.

A couple of weeks ago I sat in several sessions at the ISC2 Strategic Conference in Denver that spent a remarkable amount of time on strategies for clearly communicating risk and documenting those exchanges in much the same way as they would any other log, piece of evidence, or asset. In the past, these conversations would have been more focused on translating tech talk into corporate speak . CISOs have worked for a long time on how to talk to leadership about risk and budget; it's been an ongoing conversation for several years. However, emphasis on how cyber teams can learn to ask the right questions not just of leadership, but pertinent people both inside and outside the business, feels like a fresh effort. Using precise language and presenting strategic (not just technical and tactical) concepts effectively is no longer being discussed as a nice thing for security pros to be able to do, but critical to fundamental enterprise defense.

For example, CISO and expert Laura Vaughn has cleverly broken down threat modeling into 4 Simple Questions on a White Board . Her strategy distills years of experience and technical expertise into plain language anyone can understand, like, "What [cyber incident] would hurt most on Monday morning?" That honed language helps get teams to the heart of the threats, and helps them understand the work that needs to happen next. That all saves time and money, and eliminates the scariest risks first. Other deceptively simple questions she suggests asking include, "Who hacks organizations like ours and how?" And, "What is the cheapest control?" Smart comms informs and focuses the technical work.

Related: How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

Likewise, technologist and attorney Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, presents language as a frontline defense, and coaches CISOs and cyber leaders on the finer points of contract negotiations. He advocates rigorous documentation of communications on risk and defense decisions, so those decisions would be defensible later , and so that transparency can help drive cybersecurity across the organization.

The introduction of AI is also requiring cybersecurity teams to pick their words carefully . AI has put a language interface between the user and compute operations that benefits those who can ask the best questions. Likewise, experts across the cyber sector urge caution around using humanizing language to describe AI agents or attribute human motivation to their actions.

Related: US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Being an expert communicator is no longer a skill that's nice to have in cybersecurity; it's fundamental to enterprise defense. Be precise in the words you choose, and meet your audiences where they are. You might be surprised to find it's becoming the most powerful tool you or your organization could ever deploy against the next threat.

Just in time for the new year, Cybersecurity Outlook 2027 will look ahead at some of the newest threats posed by cybercriminals and nation-states, as well as evolving technologies that may help mitigate those threats as AI proliferates. You'll hear from some of the cybersecurity industry's leading analysts and experts, as well as researchers who have been examining the next wave of cyber threats, AI-driven technologies and other cybersecurity tools to help organizations defend their multi-cloud and hybrid environments.

Award-winning journalist and senior editor at Dark Reading reporting across diverse media platforms, including podcasts and video. Becky is passionate about delivering insightful, high-quality information and storytelling that informs and engages the cybersecurity community. Her specific focus is on the intersection of cybersecurity and public policy and its impact on the enterprise.

As the host and producer of the recently Azbee-recognized Dark Reading Confidential podcast, she presents compelling conversations with industry leaders, exploring the latest trends and challenges in cybersecurity. Becky is also the moderator Dark Reading's popular editorial webinars, and oversees Dark Reading's Commentary section, curating expert perspectives intended to drive meaningful dialogue. Additionally, she is the host of Dark Reading's Black Hat News Desk, delivering timely and in-depth coverage right from the heart of one of the industry's most important events.

Beyond editorial responsibilities, Becky is a regular writer and reporter for Dark Reading, contributing articles that delve into the evolving cybersecurity landscape.

Prior to joining Dark Reading, Becky honed her expertise as a cybersecurity reporter for Threatpost, where she covered breaking news and emerging threats in the digital security space. She holds a BA in political science from the University of Arizona, and a BA in journalism from the Walter Cronkite School of Journalism at Arizona State University.

business_items.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
business_items.summary: Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.

A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply mitigations per vendor instructions or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Microsoft SharePoint Server Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Microsoft SharePoint Server contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated attacker, who has gained access to spoofed JWT authentication tokens, to use them for executing a network attack. This attack bypasses authentication, enabling the attacker to gain administrator privileges.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply mitigations per vendor instructions or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Ivanti Connect Secure and Policy Secure Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

This vulnerability can be leveraged in conjunction with CVE-2024-21887, a command injection vulnerability.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply mitigations per vendor instructions or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.
cisa_kev_catalog.notes: Please apply mitigations per vendor instructions. For more information, please see: https://forums.ivanti.com/s/article/KB-CVE-2023-46805-Authentication-Bypass-CVE-2024-21887-Command-Injection-for-Ivanti-Connect-Secure-and-Ivanti-Policy-Secure-Gateways?language=en_US ;  https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-46805

cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply mitigations per vendor instructions or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Juniper Junos OS EX Series Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Cisco IOS XE Web UI Command Injection Vulnerability

Cisco identified CVE-2023-20273 as the vulnerability exploited to deploy the implant. CVE-2021-1435, previously associated with the exploitation events, is no longer believed to be related to this activity.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Verify that instances of Cisco IOS XE Web UI are in compliance with BOD 23-02 and apply mitigations per vendor instructions. For affected products (Cisco IOS XE Web UI exposed to the internet or to untrusted networks), follow vendor instructions to determine if a system may have been compromised and immediately report positive findings to CISA.

cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Roundcube Webmail File Disclosure Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Roundcube Webmail contains a file disclosure vulnerability caused by insufficient input validation in conjunction with file-based attachment plugins, which are used by default.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SaltStack Salt Path Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SaltStack Salt contains a path traversal vulnerability in the salt-master process ClearFuncs which allows directory access to authenticated users. Salt users who follow fundamental internet security guidelines and best practices are not affected by this vulnerability.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SaltStack Salt Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SaltStack Salt contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the salt-master process ClearFuncs due to improperly validating method calls. The vulnerability allows a remote user to access some methods without authentication, which can be used to retrieve user tokens from the salt master and/or run commands on salt minions. Salt users who follow fundamental internet security guidelines and best practices are not affected by this vulnerability.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SaltStack Salt Shell Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SaltStack Salt allows an unauthenticated user with network access to the Salt API to use shell injections to run code on the Salt API using the SSH client. This vulnerability affects any users running the Salt API.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP Customer Relationship Management (CRM) Path Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP Customer Relationship Management (CRM) contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows an attacker to exploit insufficient validation of path information provided by users.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms Invoker Servlet does not require authentication, allowing for remote code execution via a HTTP or HTTPS request.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver XML External Entity (XXE) Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms contains an unspecified vulnerability in BC-BMT-BPM-DSK which allows remote, authenticated users to conduct XML External Entity (XXE) attacks.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms contains a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability allowing unauthenticated access to execute configuration tasks and create administrative users.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP Solution Manager Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP Solution Manager User Experience Monitoring contains a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability which results in complete compromise of all SMDAgents connected to the Solution Manager.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver Directory Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms contains a directory traversal vulnerability via a ..\ (dot dot backslash) in the fileName parameter to CrashFileDownloadServlet. This allows remote attackers to read files.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SIMalliance Toolbox Browser Command Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SIMalliance Toolbox Browser contains an command injection vulnerability that could allow remote attackers to retrieve location and IMEI information or execute a range of other attacks by modifying the attack message.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SolarWinds Orion Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SolarWinds Orion API contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to execute API commands.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SolarWinds Serv-U Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SolarWinds Serv-U contains an unspecified memory escape vulnerability which can allow for remote code execution.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SolarWinds Virtualization Manager Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SolarWinds Virtualization Manager allows for privilege escalation through leveraging a misconfiguration of sudo.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Sonatype Nexus Repository Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Sonatype Nexus Repository contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall Email Security Improper Privilege Management Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall Email Security contains an improper privilege management vulnerability that allows an attacker to create an administrative account by sending a crafted HTTP request to the remote host. This vulnerability has known usage in a SonicWall Email Security exploit chain along with CVE-2021-20022 and CVE-2021-20023 to achieve privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall SMA100 SQL Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall SMA100 contains a SQL injection vulnerability allowing an unauthenticated user to gain read-only access to unauthorized resources.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall Email Security Unrestricted Upload of File Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall Email Security contains an unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability that allows a post-authenticated attacker to upload a file to the remote host. This vulnerability has known usage in a SonicWall Email Security exploit chain along with CVE-2021-20021 and CVE-2021-20023 to achieve privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall Email Security Path Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall Email Security contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows a post-authenticated attacker to read files on the remote host. This vulnerability has known usage in a SonicWall Email Security exploit chain along with CVE-2021-20021 and CVE-2021-20022 to achieve privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall SSLVPN SMA100 SQL Injection Vulnerability

cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Sophos SFOS SQL Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Sophos Firewall operating system (SFOS) firmware contains a SQL injection vulnerability when configured with either the administration (HTTPS) service or the User Portal is exposed on the WAN zone. cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Sumavision EMR Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Sumavision Enhanced Multimedia Router (EMR) contains a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerability allowing the creation of users with elevated privileges as administrator on a device.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Symantec Messaging Gateway Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Symantec Messaging Gateway contains an unspecified vulnerability which can allow for remote code execution. With the ability to perform remote code execution, an attacker may also desire to perform privilege escalating actions.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: TeamViewer Desktop Bypass Remote Login Vulnerability

If an attacker were to know this key, they could decrypt protected information stored in registry or configuration files or decryption of the Unattended Access password to the system (which allows for remote login to the system).
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX and Sitefinity Cryptographic Weakness Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX and Sitefinity have a cryptographic weakness in Telerik.Web.UI.dll that can be exploited to disclose encryption keys (Telerik.Web.UI.DialogParametersEncryptionKey and/or the MachineKey), perform cross-site-scripting (XSS) attacks, compromise the ASP.NET ViewState, and/or upload and download files.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Tenda AC11 Router Stack Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Tenda AC7, AC9, and AC10 Routers Command Injection Vulnerability

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro OfficeScan Directory Traversal Vulnerability

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Apex One and OfficeScan Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

items.details:
Attackers abused a Microsoft Store app called Setup Assistant to deploy Vinci RAT, a previously undocumented PowerShell-based remote access trojan.

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber attack in which a threat actor leveraged a Microsoft Store application to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) called Vinci RAT .

The intrusion, according to eSentire, begins with a redirection to a bogus site for a sniping tool ("snipp.codes-team[.]com"), from where a Microsoft-signed installer called "Snipping-Tool.exe" is downloaded. Executing the binary leads to the installation of Setup Assistant , an Electron-based application published on the Microsoft Store by ETPS Ltd.

"The application was heavily obfuscated, maintained communication with C2 [command-and-control] infrastructure, monitored the victim's Downloads folder, and supported execution of C2-supplied PowerShell and JavaScript," eSentire said .

"This access was used to launch a malicious PowerShell stager, establish persistence through a scheduled task, and retrieve a previously undocumented PowerShell-based RAT."

Once installed, Setup Assistant acts as a backdoor and is designed to run obfuscated JavaScript that allows it to contact the C2 server at "setup-assistant[.]com" and retrieve arbitrary PowerShell or JavaScript code, ultimately resulting in the deployment of the RAT by means of a stager.

Vinci RAT, as the malware is called, is equipped to fingerprint the host, enumerate installed security tools, facilitate remote and reverse shell access, deliver files, and execute shellcode, DLL, EXE, and PowerShell payloads.

Interestingly, the arbitrary PowerShell or JavaScript execution is triggered by means of two methods -

Monitor for file names in the victim's Downloads directory by matching them against a predefined list specified in a C2-retrieved configuration ("MSTeamsSetup.exe" and "Reader_install.exe"). If a match is found, it sends an HTTP POST request to the C2 server and executes the response.

The C2 server initiates an update action via the URL setup-assistant[.]com/api/update-status?device=<victim_id>"

The Vinci RAT stager is responsible for running a PowerShell command that disables the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface ( AMSI ), generates a unique victim identifier, establishes communication with a C2 server ("monkeysholder[.]info/api.php"), set up persistence via a scheduled task that runs every 10 minutes, and downloads the RAT payload.

Further analysis of the root domain " codes-team[.]com " has identified additional sub-domains that suggest that the threat actors are spoofing software download pages for legitimate applications like Microsoft Teams and Roblox -

As of writing, Setup Assistant is no longer accessible on Microsoft Software. It was first released on June 1, 2026, while the "codes-team[.]com" domain was registered in late March 2026.

It remains unclear whether the threat actors themselves took down the app in response to the public disclosure or whether Microsoft removed it, as eSentire noted that the tech giant had failed to take action despite reporting the app through its abuse form on November 10, 2026, responding that it was "not a violation of our terms."

"The campaign highlights how attackers are combining search-engine redirection, fake software download pages, obfuscated Electron applications, and trusted software distribution channels to gain persistent access to victim environments," the Canadian cybersecurity company said.

items.title: Microsoft removes WSUS server role in Windows Server 2028
items.summary: Microsoft will remove the WSUS server role from Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system. [...]
items.details:
Microsoft will remove the WSUS server role from Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system.

Introduced in 2005 as Software Update Services (SUS), WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) lets IT administrators manage and distribute updates for Microsoft products across corporate networks with many Windows devices.

It gives admins centralized control over the updates, rather than having each device download them individually from Microsoft's servers.

Microsoft has officially deprecated WSUS in September 2024 , but said that it still plans to maintain functionality and continue publishing updates through the channel. The change affects enterprise environments that rely on WSUS to manage updates delivered to many devices but does not impact home users or those using Microsoft Configuration Manager.

In a recently updated support document, Microsoft went even further and confirmed that Windows Server 2028 removes the WSUS server role altogether.

"WSUS remains available and supported in earlier Windows Server releases, including Windows Server 2025, for the duration of each release's support lifecycle. You can continue to use WSUS on those releases to manage updates for supported Windows client and Windows Server releases, which includes updates to Windows Server 2028," it said .

"Microsoft recognizes the need to manage updates in disconnected and highly controlled environments. We're invested in supporting these scenarios and we'll share more as the work progresses."

Businesses are now encouraged to adopt cloud-based solutions, such as Windows Autopatch, Microsoft Intune, and Azure Update Manager, for keeping endpoints and servers on their network up to date.

"While the WSUS role remains available in Windows Server 2025, we recommend organizations transition to cloud tools, including including Windows Autopatch and Microsoft Intune for client update management and Azure Update Manager for server update management," Microsoft's Nir Froimovici said in September 2024. "Remember: WSUS remains operational but is no longer investing in new features."

Windows Server 2028 also removes VBScript ( disabled by default in Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10) and the legacy Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line (WMIC) utility ( deprecated in Windows Server 2012 and Windows 10 21H1) to thwart a wide range of malware and attack tactics abusing them.

Windows Internet Name Service (WINS) support, deprecated with the release of Windows Server 2022 in August 2021, is also being removed in the next Windows Server version, as Microsoft announced a year ago .

Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028 last week at the Ignite 2026 conference, and it can be tested by registering for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or applying to enroll in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access.

items.title: How to Keep Your Security Picture Current When Attackers Move at AI Speed
items.summary: Most security metrics are not built to be used. They are built to be shown. items.details:
Continuous security posture visibility helps teams address outdated metrics, fragmented data, and the growing pace of AI-accelerated threats.

Most security metrics are not built to be used. They are built to be shown. Somewhere between the quarterly review and the next status update, a set of numbers gets assembled that looks reassuring in a room and tells almost no one what is actually happening across the environment that week. Someone pulls them together the week before, cleans them up, and presents a picture of a program that is, as of that one morning, fine.

This is not a failure of effort. Security teams are doing the work, often times more of it than anyone outside the team realizes. The problem is that the reporting cycle rewards the snapshot, and a snapshot is a memory, not a measurement. It tells you how things looked on the day you looked. It says very little about the weeks in between, and risk does not keep to a reporting schedule.

The conversation about security metrics usually jumps straight to which numbers matter. That skips the part that actually hurts. Before anyone can report a single metric, someone has to go and gather it, and today that is a genuinely painful job.

The information needed to describe a security posture is scattered across dozens of systems that were never meant to talk to each other. Cloud accounts, identity providers, endpoints, code repositories, ticketing tools, each one holds a piece. Pulling those pieces together usually means logging into one console after another, exporting spreadsheets, taking screenshots, and stitching it all by hand into something presentable. It takes days. It eats the time of people who were hired to do security, not data entry. And by the time the picture is assembled, parts of it are already out of date, because the environment kept changing while the deck was being built.

So the metric that lands in the review is not really a measurement of where things stand. It is a measurement of where things stood, filtered through however long it took to collect. (And filtered, quietly, toward whatever looked defensible that week.)

Here is why the stale snapshot has gone from a weakness to a real liability. The people trying to get in have changed speed.

AI has handed attackers a serious acceleration. Reconnaissance that used to take a skilled operator days now runs in minutes. Phishing that used to read as obviously fake now arrives fluent and personalized at scale. Known weaknesses get found and probed almost as fast as they appear. The attack side has automated the slow parts, and the result is adversaries who move in hours, iterate constantly, and do not pause politely between your reporting cycles.

Now put the two timelines next to each other. On one side, a picture of your security that is gathered by hand, a few times a year, and is slightly stale the moment it is finished. On the other, an adversary moving at machine speed, every day, including the long quiet stretch between your last review and your next one. That gap was always uncomfortable. Against AI-accelerated attackers, it is the whole game.

The fix is not a better slide. It is being able to see where you actually stand, continuously, without a person having to go assemble it first.

That is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to confuse with detection. This is not about catching the attacker in the act. It is about never losing sight of your own environment in the first place, knowing what you have, what is covered, what changed, and where the gaps are, as a living picture rather than a quarterly photograph. Continuous visibility into the real environment, pulled straight from the systems that already hold the data, is what turns a security posture from something you reconstruct under deadline into something you can simply look at, any day, and trust.

This is the problem Anecdotes was built to solve. Instead of a person logging into one console after another and rebuilding the picture by hand, it connects directly to the systems a company already runs, the cloud accounts, identity providers, code repositories, and the hundreds of other tools where the real state actually lives, and pulls the information straight from the source. The picture assembles itself and stays current, so the question stops being how many days it will take to gather and becomes simply what the data says right now. And to be clear about what that is and is not, it does not chase the attacker for you. It makes sure you are never the last to know what your own environment looks like.

When the picture is always current, the work changes shape. Nobody spends the week before the review gathering. The number is just there, today's number, and the team spends its time acting on what it says instead of proving it exists.

None of this requires rebuilding everything at once, and anyone who says it does is selling something. Pick one thing worth seeing clearly, coverage, say, or how long exposures stay open. Connect it to the source so it keeps itself current. Watch it for a month, and let it tell you something uncomfortable.

Security is not a thing that is true on review day. It is true, or it is not, on an ordinary Tuesday, when no one is looking and last quarter's slide is gathering dust in a shared drive. And on that Tuesday, the attackers are not waiting. The teams that stay ahead are not the ones with the best-looking dashboards. They are the ones who can see where they stand at any moment, without having to go dig for it first.

items.title: Drupal warns of new site takeover flaw exploited in attacks
items.summary: The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites. [...]
items.details:
The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites.

Last week, Drupal patched a remote code execution (RCE) flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165 / Fail2Install ) that lets anonymous users take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.

While the security issue wasn't initially flagged as being abused in the wild, an update to the original security advisory warned that threat actors began exploiting it one day after patches were released.

The new security issue ( CVE-2026-136716 ), patched one week later, addresses attack vectors that were left unpatched and also lets attackers hijack vulnerable Drupal sites.

"However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state," Drupal said on Wednesday.

"This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised."

While it has yet to share further details regarding these attacks, Drupal warned users that any unsecured website may have been compromised and advised admins to ensure the user 1 email address is one they control, and to consider resetting it.

They should also check site logs for unauthorized access, focusing on unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account, and follow this guide if they find evidence the site may have been compromised.

Those who can't immediately upgrade to Drupal 10.6.23 , 11.3.23 , or 11.4.14 should secure the installer on all new and existing sites by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged six Drupal security flaws as being abused in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been exploited in ransomware attacks.

items.title: SAP confirms security incident after suspicious GitHub activity
items.summary: SAP has confirmed to BleepingComputer that it took urgent action to protect its customers after detecting suspicious activity in its IT environment. [...]
items.details:
SAP has confirmed to BleepingComputer that it took urgent action to protect its customers after detecting suspicious activity in its IT environment.

The German software giant said its evidence so far does not show downstream compromise of customer systems or data.

Based in Walldorf, Germany, SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software vendors, with 110,000 employees in 157 countries, 300 million subscribers, and over $40 billion in annual revenue .

Der Spiegel reported earlier today, based on an internal SAP memo it saw, that the software firm was hit by a cyberattack it tracks under the code name “Project Granite.”

The software company reportedly asked all employees to keep the project details confidential.

According to the German outlet, sources within the company said the attackers breached SAP’s GitHub environment, possibly with help from AI tools.

Insider sources say that the attacker managed to steal authentication tokens from SAP employees and leveraged them to copy and also modify SAP source code on GitHub.

BleepingComputer has contacted SAP for a statement on the reported breach, and the company acknowledged the incident and said it had taken steps to protect its customers.

“SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services,” a company representative told BleepingComputer.

“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.”

“Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.”

SAP did not specify the environments where the suspicious activity was observed, or whether customers downloading code from its GitHub repositories or performing updates that are directly fetched or indirectly fed by those repositories should take any action.

BleepingComputer has asked SAP about this, but a spokesperson declined to share any further information.

Meanwhile, Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) issued a public warning yesterday about agentic AI tools that empower cyberattacks, such as ARTEX, CAIRN, and PentAGI.

BSI cautioned organizations in the country to focus on responding to security incidents and ensure they follow all recommended security-strengthening practices.

This warning comes shortly after the national cybersecurity agencies in Switzerland and Italy reported the first detections of large-scale AI-driven cyberattacks targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector.

items.title: Hackers Trojanize Official Q-Dir and DesktopOK Downloads to Deliver Remote Access Malware
items.summary: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a software supply chain attack that has tampered with Q-Dir and DesktopOK installation files distributed via the official SoftwareOK website. "Evidence indicates that malicious files were generated not only when users downloaded the programs directly from the official download page but also during the update process of previously installed
items.details:
Trojanized Q-Dir and DesktopOK installers from SoftwareOK's official website deploy a Python RAT capable of remote command execution.

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a software supply chain attack that has tampered with Q-Dir and DesktopOK installation files distributed via the official SoftwareOK website.

"Evidence indicates that malicious files were generated not only when users downloaded the programs directly from the official download page but also during the update process of previously installed legitimate programs," South Korean cybersecurity company AhnLab said .

Q-Dir, also called the Quad Directory Explorer, is a free, lightweight file manager for Windows developed by SoftwareOK. According to its website, DesktopOK is a free Windows utility designed to save and restore desktop icon positions.

The unauthorized modifications are designed such that the malicious activity is challenging to detect when running the programs, while simultaneously retrieving and deploying a Python-based remote control malware (RAT) from an external server.

Once installed, the RAT payload is capable of executing shell commands and Python code, transferring files, capturing screenshots, and collecting system metadata based on commands issued by the attacker.

The following product versions have been confirmed to be poisoned, given the discrepancies in the SHA-256 hashes of the installer files and the presence of additional code that triggers additional file downloads and automatic execution -

The exact mechanism that allowed the installation files to be replaced with a trojanized version remains unknown.

"The malicious installer runs the legitimate Q-Dir or DesktopOK to lower the user's suspicion, while simultaneously downloading and installing a Python RAT package from an external server," AhnLab said.

Specifically, this involves downloading two payloads from "mail.c1a2[.]top" -

dsv2_py39_agent.7z, a package containing the RAT and Python runtime environment

The attack chain is fairly straightforward in that it uses the 7-Zip tool binary to extract and run the Python RAT. The malware then sets up persistence on the host by means of a scheduled task that impersonates Microsoft Edge to fly under the radar. The task is configured to execute the RAT by launching a Python script named "py_client_dsv2.py."

Upon execution, the RAT establishes communication with its command-and-control (C2) server ("8.210.69[.]51:9876") to receive tasks and run them. It supports the following features -

It also gathers a list of running processes and compares it against an internal list of various security products used in South Korea and abroad, including AhnLab, ESTSecurity, Hauri, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Trend Micro, Avast, McAfee, ESET, Symantec, Kaspersky, Bitdefender, Sophos, Fortinet, Elastic, and Malwarebytes.

Information about identified security programs is transmitted to the C2 server, so as to help the attackers better plan the next stages of the attack or serve payloads that can bypass detection.

The activity has not been attributed to any known threat actor. However, AhnLab said it identified Chinese language comments in the source code, suggesting that the malware authors or attackers may have used a Chinese-speaking environment.

"Users who are currently using Q-Dir or DesktopOK, or who have recently installed or updated these programs, should verify the hash values of the downloaded files and check their systems for any traces of RAT installation or execution," AhnLab said.

"However, simply uninstalling and reinstalling the program may not remove a Python RAT that has already been installed. Therefore, you should also check for suspicious Python execution environments, scheduled tasks, related files, and traces of external network communication, update your antivirus engine to the latest version, and then perform a full system scan."

items.title: Microsoft pushes emergency hotpatch to fix Windows Server crashes
items.summary: Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update (KB5131077). [...]
items.details:
Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update (KB5131077).

Microsoft has released an emergency hotpatch update to address Windows Server 2025 crashes triggered after installing this month's security hotpatch update ( KB5131077 ).

According to Microsoft, the KB5138318 out-of-band update should address stop errors with 0x139 codes triggered on affected servers when IPv6 routes expire.

"Microsoft has released a new Windows out-of-band (OOB) update today, November 25, 2026, to address an issue affecting a limited number of Windows Servers with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes," it said in a message center update.

"Affected devices might stop unexpectedly with stop error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE) when a route timer expires. This issue affects some Windows Server 2025 devices after installing the November 2026 Windows security hotpatch update."

This emergency non-security update is now rolling out to affected Windows Server 2025 devices enrolled in hotpatch updates through Windows Update.

KB5138318 will download and install automatically and will take effect without requiring IT administrators or users to restart affected devices.

The November 2026 hotpatch updates are also causing issues for Windows 11 users, who are experiencing installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications, as well as printing issues on systems running Forcepoint's DLP Endpoint Agent data loss prevention solution after installing this month's hotpatch on Windows 11 systems.

Windows Autopatch reached public preview in early June after an initial unveil in April 2022 and has been generally available since July 2022 .

Microsoft announced earlier this year, in March, that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed.

One month later, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that was causing driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices in the European Union.

items.title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges
items.summary: ​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges. [...]
items.details:
​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges.

Found by ANSSI's Jérémy Jean (who submitted a fix in August ), the flaw has been dubbed NFS2ROOT by cybersecurity firm OpenSec, which shared a full remote-root exploit and a patch with the NFSD maintainers in late September.

The vulnerability has existed since Linux kernel version 3.16 ( released in March 2014 ), and it stems from a heap buffer overflow weakness in the Linux NFS server (nfsd).

NFS2ROOT affects systems with a Linux kernel older than 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, or 7.4-rc1 if nfsd (v4.1 or 4.2) is loaded and running and TCP port 2049 is reachable over the Internet.

Successful exploitation lets remote threat actors without privileges corrupt kernel memory and gain root access to vulnerable Linux servers exposed online through low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction.

In NFS2ROOT attacks, the threat actors can exploit this flaw by sending maliciously crafted requests that cause the NFS server to write data beyond an allocated memory buffer. This lets them read kernel memory, bypass KASLR (which protects kernel memory addresses), and place a callback that can execute a command in a released memory area.

When the attacker closes the NFS connection, the kernel executes the embedded command with root privileges, allowing the attacker to gain root control of the unpatched Linux server.

​Although there are no reports of CVE-2026-99362 exploitation in the wild, security teams should apply the latest kernel security updates from their Linux distribution vendor immediately to block potential attacks, then reboot the system to ensure the patched kernel is in use.

Those who can't apply a patch immediately should restrict access to the NFS server over TCP port 2049 to trusted clients or networks. Additionally, if NFS sharing is not required on the system, admins can stop and disable the nfs-server service in /etc/nfs.conf.

"Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in," OpenSec said . "Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host."

While the NFS2ROOT attacks have no network signatures, security teams can still monitor for potential signs of exploitation attempts by checking for kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server, bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source, and kernel oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames, according to OpenSec.

NFS2ROOT is the latest in a long series of Linux privilege escalation security flaws disclosed and patched since the start of the year, including RefluXFS , CIFSwitch , Dirty Frag , Fragnesia , PinTheft , Copy Fail , Pack2TheRoot , and DirtyDecrypt/DirtyCBC .

items.title: Switzerland Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattacks Breached Critical Infrastructure Operators
items.summary: Attackers using AI agents have broken into computer systems at Swiss organizations in four of five confirmed attacks, the first such cases in the country, the country's cybersecurity agency said yesterday.
